html:
In the 1500s farmers in the lands of the Republic of Venice began to sow whole fields of maize, a crop from the Americas brought over in the Columbian Exchange. It gave far more grain per field than wheat or millet.

The historian Fernand Braudel uses Venetia as an example of how a new crop changed the countryside. Maize ended local famines, but it also changed what the poor ate. Peasants lived on maize porridge, polenta, and sold their wheat to the city, where it fetched a better price.

There was a cost. A diet of little but maize lacks a vitamin, and by the 1700s and 1800s the disease pellagra was common among the poor of northern Italy. The same pattern of a high yield American crop feeding a growing population appeared elsewhere, as when maize reached China and the potato spread across Europe.
